setup.en: At a Sioux Falls grocery checkout, a school cook separates onions from a sprawling receipt.

text.en: South Dakota voters rejected Initiated Measure 28 in 2024. It proposed barring state taxes on many human-consumption goods, excluding alcohol and prepared food.

comment.en: “The grocery-tax repeal lost. State still comes to dinner. Never chops an onion, never washes a plate, always gets served before I do.”

sources.title: South Dakota Secretary of State: 2024 Ballot Questions
sources.qualification: Official result: Measure 28 failed, 129,261 to 290,969. The proposal was broader than groceries alone; no claim that it would have eliminated every local tax.

sources.title: South Dakota 2024 General Election Ballot Question Pamphlet
sources.qualification: Attorney General’s explanation describes the state-tax proposal and excludes alcoholic beverages and prepared food. Competing campaign arguments are not treated as established facts.

setup.en: At a Sioux Falls feed-store bench, a farmhand discusses the state’s pipeline law.

text.en: In March 2025, Governor Rhoden barred eminent domain for carbon-oxide pipelines in South Dakota, preventing compulsory land acquisition for those projects while allowing voluntary deals.

comment.en: “Rhoden blocked forced land-taking for carbon pipelines. A private company has been invited to try the free market. We wish it a speedy recovery.”

sources.title: South Dakota Governor: Rhoden Signs Property Rights Bill
sources.qualification: Primary source; dated or historical action only.

sources.title: South Dakota2025Session Law Chapter190
sources.qualification: Restricts eminentdomain for carbon-oxide pipelines, not every pipeline or voluntary easement.

title.en: The Hiring Freeze Found the Kitchen

setup.en: At a South Bend café, a campus kitchen worker tells you about Notre Dame’s budget notice.

text.en: In June 2025, Notre Dame announced a 2.5% budget reduction and continued its hiring freeze amid Trump-era federal funding and tax uncertainty.

comment.en: “Trump’s funding and tax uncertainty put campus hiring on ice. The dishes still arrive hot. Washington has created a hiring freeze with excellent steam.”

sources.title: Notre Dame’s Response to Federal Funding Cuts
sources.qualification: Campus reporting verified through indexed text. Uses the June 19, 2025 budget announcement, not the article’s inconsistent March statement date.

setup.en: Outside South Bend’s auto museum, a retired machinist shares a bench with you.

text.en: Studebaker’s 1963 closure left nearly 3,000 South Bend workers without pension benefits, fueling reform. Congress’s 1974 ERISA law later set minimum standards for private retirement plans.

comment.en: “Congress tightened pension rules after Studebaker workers lost benefits. Revolutionary idea: retirement money should survive the company’s final management decision.”

sources.title: US Department of Labor: Studebaker Plant Closes
sources.qualification: Primary source; dated or historical action only.

sources.title: US Department of Labor: ERISA
sources.qualification: Minimum standards for covered private plans, not an unlimited federal guarantee of all benefits.

setup.en: At a South Bend grocery bench, a campus cleaner compares bank fees with the university’s tax fight.

text.en: In 2025, Notre Dame joined other faith-based institutions seeking a religious exemption from higher endowment-return taxes. The final federal legislation included no such exemption.

comment.en: “Notre Dame sought religious relief on investment taxes. I asked if my overdraft was also a matter of faith. The bank believes in fees.”

sources.title: Notre Dame’s Response to Federal Funding Cuts
sources.qualification: Campus reporting verified through indexed text. Uses the June 19, 2025 budget announcement, not the article’s inconsistent March statement date.

setup.en: At a Spokane shaded bus stop, a renter uses a folded paper as a fan.

text.en: In September 2025, Spokane reported that Trump’s administration rescinded a $19.9 million grant supporting planned heating, cooling and air-filter improvements for 300 low-income homes.

comment.en: “Trump’s administration rescinded the home-cooling grant. The heat kept its funding. I am applying to become a federally recognized breeze.”

sources.title: Proposed Resolution Outlines City of Spokane’s Federal Priorities
sources.qualification: City account of rescinded awards; home upgrades were planned, not reported completed.

setup.en: At a Spokane laundromat, a delivery worker compares a rent notice with a pay slip.

text.en: Governor Bob Ferguson signed Washington’s rent-stabilization law in May 2025, limiting increases for covered existing tenants to 7% plus inflation or 10%, whichever is lower.

comment.en: “Ferguson capped rent hikes. Good. My landlord’s ceiling now rises more slowly than before, which is helpful because my paycheck still cannot reach it.”

sources.title: Governor Ferguson Signs Rent Stabilization Bills
sources.qualification: Primary source; dated or historical action only.

sources.title: Washington Commerce: HB1217 Resource Center
sources.qualification: Caps apply to covered tenancies with exemptions; not a rent freeze or a claim the maximum is charged to every tenant.

title.en: Free Speech Had a Placement Fee

setup.en: On a Spokane downtown bench, a warehouse worker explains the city’s old street-speaking ban.

text.en: After Spokane workers protested exploitative job-placement practices, employment-agency owners persuaded city officials to prohibit street speaking, helping trigger the city’s free-speech struggle.

comment.en: “Job agencies sold lousy jobs; workers complained. Spokane restricted street speaking. The city solved the employment problem by regulating the people describing it.”

sources.title: IWW formally begins Spokane free-speech fight on November 2, 1909.
sources.qualification: HistoryLink historical account; agency practices and the city speech ordinance are historical, not present-day allegations.

setup.en: Near Lincoln Home in Springfield, a cleaner recalls the shutdown while you rest by the neighborhood fence.

text.en: On October 1, 2025, the federal shutdown closed Lincoln Home’s visitor center and house tours in Springfield, while the neighborhood grounds remained open.

comment.en: “Congress shut down government and Lincoln tours closed. You could admire democracy through the window. Please do not touch; it was a display model.”

sources.title: Lincoln Home site closed until further notice amid government shutdown
sources.qualification: WAND indexed article verified; closure is the October 2025 announcement, not a claim of current closure. Grounds remained accessible.

title.en: No Doctor’s Note for Being Alive

setup.en: At a Springfield laundromat, a cook plans a day off while your blankets dry.

text.en: Illinois’s paid-leave law took effect in 2024, allowing covered workers to earn up to forty hours annually for any reason, subject to its eligibility and notice rules.

comment.en: “Illinois lets covered workers earn leave for any reason. My boss asked why. I showed him the law. He prefers laws with fewer employees in them.”

sources.title: Illinois General Assembly: Paid Leave for All Workers Act
sources.qualification: Covered workers accrue leave; the law has exclusions and does not grant every worker an immediate forty-hour bank.

setup.en: At a Springfield grocery checkout, an off-duty stocker compares your food total with an hourly wage.

text.en: Illinois’s state minimum wage reached $15 an hour for covered workers aged eighteen and older on January 1, 2025.

comment.en: “Illinois raised the adult minimum to fifteen dollars. Funny how wages needed legislation while the grocery prices managed their promotion without a single hearing.”

sources.title: Illinois Department of Labor: Minimum Wage FAQ
sources.qualification: Adult covered-worker rate; tipped and under-eighteen rules differ.

setup.en: At a Springfield food pantry bench, a delivery worker talks about missing federal orders.

text.en: In March 2025, Springfield’s Ozarks Food Harvest estimated that Trump’s USDA cancellations would remove $3 million in food that year; one-third of canceled orders were protein foods.

comment.en: “Trump’s USDA canceled three million dollars in food. A third was protein. The pantry has plenty of explanations, but nobody has found a recipe yet.”

sources.title: Ozarks Food Harvest will lose $3 million in food from USDA cuts this year
sources.qualification: Foodbank’s contemporaneous estimate for 2025, not a retrospective measurement; one-third of canceled orders were protein foods.

setup.en: At a Springfield grocery bench, a cleaner checks a pay slip against your receipt.

text.en: Governor Kehoe’s 2025 legislation removed future inflation indexing from Missouri’s minimum wage while keeping the scheduled increase to $15 in 2026.

comment.en: “Kehoe removed automatic inflation raises from Missouri’s minimum wage. I asked the cereal to cooperate. It says its lobbyist is handling the matter.”

sources.title: Governor Kehoe Signs Tax Cuts and Pro-Business Legislation
sources.qualification: Primary source; dated or historical action only.

setup.en: At a Springfield utility-work fence, an installer pauses while you check your route.

text.en: Springfield’s community-owned City Utilities built a fiber expansion exceeding 1,000 miles by 2023. Private broadband providers lease that public infrastructure to deliver service.

comment.en: “The city utility built the fiber; private providers lease it and sell service. Even the invisible hand needs the public to run its cables.”

sources.title: City Utilities Annual Report 2022
sources.qualification: Utility report identifies Brightspeed and a second tenant on SpringNet fiber infrastructure.

sources.title: City Utilities Annual Report 2023
sources.qualification: Utility reports its fiber expansion completed in May 2023 and added over 1,000 miles; figures refer to that project.

sources.title: About City Utilities
sources.qualification: Primary source establishes that City Utilities is community-owned.

setup.en: At a St. Louis grocery exit, a food-bank driver describes the canceled Illinois purchasing round.

text.en: In May 2025, St. Louis Area Foodbank said Trump’s administration canceled its next federal local-farm purchasing round for Illinois; earlier awards could still be spent.

comment.en: “Trump canceled the next local-farm food round. The last one can finish. Apparently hunger is supposed to respect the end of a fiscal paragraph.”

sources.title: Growth and Adaptation: May at the Foodbank
sources.qualification: Foodbank states its LFPA participation was in Illinois only; existing rounds remained authorized, while the third round was canceled.

title.en: The State Stops Charging by the Diaper

setup.en: At a St. Louis grocery bench, a cleaner compares baby supplies with your small food purchase.

text.en: Missouri’s 2025 tax legislation created sales-tax exemptions for diapers and certain other personal-care necessities, reducing tax on qualifying everyday purchases.

comment.en: “Missouri removed sales tax from diapers. At last, the state admitted this transaction already produces enough waste without its contribution.”

sources.title: Governor Kehoe Signs Tax Cuts and Pro-Business Legislation
sources.qualification: Primary source; dated or historical action only.

setup.en: At a St. Louis copy shop, a delivery driver lays a parking notice beside a savings statement.

text.en: St. Louis lists a $20 meter fine that doubles after 30 days and reaches $80 after 45 days.

comment.en: “Twenty dollars grows into eighty in forty-five days. I keep the ticket next to my savings statement. Maybe it’ll teach it something.”

sources.title: City of St. Louis: Parking Violation Fines
sources.qualification: Applies to the listed meter violation and payment intervals. No claim that the resident has obtained any investment return or that the rule covers every citation.

setup.en: At a Toledo print shop’s public counter, a worker discusses tariff surcharges while you buy a postcard.

text.en: In April 2025, a Toledo-area envelope maker said a US paper supplier planned a tariff surcharge because some raw materials came from abroad.

comment.en: “Trump says tariffs protect American business. Our American paper supplier added a surcharge. The envelope industry finally has an answer to what is inside: another bill.”

sources.title: Local businesses brace for tariffs
sources.qualification: A reported supplier surcharge and local business account, not a claim about every printer or paper supplier.

setup.en: At a Toledo diner, a cleaner recalls Ohio’s decision to use unclaimed funds for football.

text.en: Governor Mike DeWine’s 2025 Ohio budget set aside $600 million in unclaimed funds for a new Cleveland Browns stadium, making a statewide fund part of the stadium plan.

comment.en: “DeWine put unclaimed money toward the Browns’ stadium. I lose twenty dollars and retrace my steps. Ohio finds six hundred million and buys football architecture.”

sources.title: AP: Ohio Budget Includes Stadium Funding
sources.qualification: Dated budget allocation; not a claim every legal challenge was resolved or the money had all been spent.

title.en: The Public Bought Back the Ground

setup.en: At Toledo’s Glass City Metropark, a groundskeeper rests while you share some food.

text.en: In 2022 and 2023, Metroparks Toledo used clean harbor-dredged sediment to help restore former industrial ground at Glass City Metropark and its Riverwalk.

comment.en: “Metroparks used clean harbor mud to rebuild industrial ground. Government turned dredging into a park. Industry had spent years demonstrating the reverse procedure.”

sources.title: Removal Recommendation: Restrictions on Navigational Dredging Activities in the Maumee Area of Concern
sources.qualification: Ohio environmental restoration report hosted by Partners for Clean Streams; describes clean harbor sediment reused at Glass City Metropark in 2022–2023.

setup.en: At a Tucson shaded food stop, a city maintenance worker checks a blank phone screen.

text.en: Tucson’s April 2025 budget memo reported federal grant portals repeatedly shutting and reopening under Trump; nearly 200 grant-funded jobs could be at risk if support disappeared.

comment.en: “Trump’s grant portals kept shutting. Nearly two hundred jobs faced funding risk. New job description: convince a website that Tucson still exists.”

sources.title: City of Tucson: Recommended Fiscal Year 2026 Budget, April 22 Study Session
sources.qualification: Page 1 of the manager’s memorandum reports portal disruptions and conditional risk to nearly 200 grant-funded positions; it does not report 200 layoffs.

title.en: The Country Club Gets the Second Sip

setup.en: At a Tucson park drinking fountain, a groundskeeper explains the separate irrigation system.

text.en: Tucson invested in reclaimed water in 1984 to reduce groundwater use. Its municipal system sends treated wastewater to irrigate parks, schools, golf courses and cemeteries.

comment.en: “The city sends treated wastewater to parks and golf courses. Sensible. The country club can have my old water; I am keeping the first sip.”

sources.title: Reclaimed Water — City of Tucson
sources.qualification: Primary utility account of investment beginning in 1984 and reclaimed irrigation for parks, schools, golf courses and cemeteries; not drinking-water guidance.

title.en: The Pentagon Needs a Parts Tray

setup.en: At a Tucson public overlook near the aircraft-storage area, a mechanic shares a snack with you.

text.en: Tucson’s military aircraft yard salvages reusable parts. In March 2025, senior Trump officials, including Pete Hegseth, discussed military strike plans in a Signal chat that accidentally included a journalist.

comment.en: “I count spare bolts before a repair. Hegseth’s strike-planning chat included a journalist. Maybe the Pentagon needs one of my little trays.”

sources.title: Signal airstrike chat
sources.qualification: In March 2025 senior Trump officials shared Yemen strike details in a Signal chat that accidentally included a journalist. Fictional workers and dialogue are invented.

setup.en: At a Tulsa clinic’s outdoor bench, a cleaner discusses the health department’s funding worries.

text.en: In March 2025, Tulsa health officials faced uncertainty over Trump-era federal support. Grants had provided over $13 million, about 30% of department revenue, in fiscal 2023–24.

comment.en: “Trump’s cuts have health officials guessing what Washington will fund. I asked whether uncertainty is contagious. They need a grant to find out.”

sources.title: Tulsa Health Department braces for an unknown future
sources.qualification: Public Radio Tulsa reporting describes uncertainty, not a confirmed $13 million loss; revenue figures refer to fiscal 2023–2024.

setup.en: At a Tulsa grocery loading area, a warehouse worker peers into a shopping bag beside your parked van.

text.en: Oklahoma ended the state sales tax on qualifying groceries on August 29, 2024; local grocery sales taxes remain.

comment.en: “State grocery tax is gone. Local tax stayed. I shook the bag to make sure. One level of government was still in there.”

sources.title: Oklahoma Tax Commission: State Sales Tax on Food and Food Ingredients
sources.qualification: State exemption for qualifying groceries; local taxes and excluded categories remain. No invented local rate or claim that all food purchases are tax-free.

setup.en: At a Tulsa bus-stop bench, a school bus driver compares the state’s video order with your route.

text.en: In November 2024, Oklahoma superintendent Ryan Walters directed schools to show students his video announcing a Department of Religious Freedom and Patriotism. Some districts refused.

comment.en: “Walters required schools to show his religious-freedom video. My kid asked if she could skip it. Excellent question for the civics final.”

sources.title: AP: Oklahoma Superintendent Orders Religious Department Video
sources.qualification: The order and resistance are documented; no claim it was universally obeyed or remains current policy.

title.en: Half the Benefits, Twice the Sandwich

setup.en: At a Waco food pantry bench, a cook recalls November’s delayed food assistance.

text.en: On November 4, 2025, KWBU reported over 31,000 McLennan County residents lacked November SNAP access during the shutdown; half payments were announced, but arrival remained unclear.

comment.en: “Washington announced half the benefits. I cut one sandwich into two. Same accounting method, but mine comes with crusts.”

sources.title: Central Texas Food Banks brace for surge after SNAP benefits cut
sources.qualification: Contemporaneous shutdown report: more than 31,000 McLennan County residents faced interrupted November benefits; half payments were announced but timing remained unclear.

setup.en: By Waco’s suspension bridge, a delivery driver pauses while you eat some food.

text.en: Waco’s 1866 toll-bridge charter barred competing bridges and ferries within five miles. McLennan County bought it in 1889, and it became a free city crossing.

comment.en: “Texas gave this toll bridge a five-mile monopoly. Free enterprise first required a law banning the competition. The public later had to buy its way out.”

sources.title: The Waco Suspension Bridge — Texas Historical Commission marker
sources.qualification: State historical marker records the 1866 monopoly charter, five-mile exclusion, and 1889 transfer to public ownership as a free bridge.

setup.en: At a Waco grocery bench, a school aide discusses Texas’s classroom-poster law.

text.en: Governor Abbott signed Texas’s 2025 law requiring Ten Commandments posters in public-school classrooms. Implementation faced legal challenges and was temporarily blocked in some districts.

comment.en: “Abbott required classroom Ten Commandments. My kid asked whether the rule against lying applies to campaign ads. We have been discussing jurisdiction.”
